title: Analyzing Learning-Dynamics Across Loss and Prediction Choices for Diffusion Models
claim: Under a low-rank bottleneck, noise and velocity prediction hit a theoretical error floor while clean-data prediction exploits low-dimensional structure.
layout: 3 line-plot panels in a row, log-scale MSE vs bottleneck dimension, dashed bound
description: Three side-by-side line plots share the x-axis, bottleneck dimension m, from about 2 to 64, with MSE on a log y-axis. The left panel, titled 'MSE vs Bottleneck Dimension (D=64, d=2)', has a flat blue x-prediction curve near the bottom. Orange eps-prediction and green v-prediction curves decline slowly from the top. A black dashed theoretical lower bound D-m drops vertically near m=48. The middle and right panels decompose eps- and v-prediction MSE into total, null-space (red) and range-space (purple) components. In both, the null-space error collapses sharply at m=64 while the total stays high. The eye goes first to the dashed bound and the flat blue line. A fragment of a results table is visible at the top of the crop.
caption: Synthetic validation of the bottleneck lower bound ([ref]) with $D=64$ and $d=2$. Left: Prediction MSE in each target's native space as a function of bottleneck dimension $m$. The $\epsilon$- and $v$-prediction errors are bounded below by $D-m$ (dashed), while $x$-prediction maintains low error for $m\geq d$. Middle, Right: Decomposition of the prediction MSE into null-space and range-space components for $\epsilon$- and $v$-prediction, respectively.
abstract: Denoising generative models predict clean data ($x$), noise ($Îµ$), or velocity ($v$), while training losses can be measured in any of these spaces. Although the resulting nine combinations are algebraically related, they can yield substantially different denoising accuracy and sample quality. We disentangle the effects of prediction and loss spaces. For a fixed prediction target, we show that changing the loss space is exactly equivalent to timestep reweighting and provide a heuristic analysis of how this reweighting affects generation quality. We then show that a rank-$m$ linear bottleneck compressing a $D$-dimensional noisy input imposes an irreducible squared-error floor of $D-m$ on noise and velocity prediction, whereas clean-data prediction can exploit low-dimensional data structure. Combining this bound with prediction-dependent error conversion yields distinct necessary conditions on bottleneck capacity. Experiments with U-Net and JiT across CIFAR-10, Imagenette, and ImageNet-256 support these theoretical predictions. Under compression, prediction choice strongly affects both denoising accuracy and sample quality, with noise-prediction errors closely matching the theoretical lower bound. Our results provide a quantitative understanding of how architectural bottlenecks interact with prediction and loss choices in denoising generative models.
